title: Voice Agent Engineering — Nik Caryotakis, SuperDial

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The entire talk is about building and scaling voice AI systems using STT/LLM/TTS stacks, voice-to-voice models, and real-time speech interaction for phone call automation. SuperDial automates enterprise healthcare back-office phone calls requiring HIPAA-compliant infrastructure and EHR integrations. The system is deployed in production, having saved over 100,000 hours of human calling time with a lean team of four engineers. The talk assumes familiarity with voice AI components and agentic systems while covering practical engineering tradeoffs, stack selection, and testing strategies. This is a recorded conference presentation from the AI Engineer Summit 2025 in New York. Multiple direct transcript quotes spanning voice AI architecture, healthcare compliance, latency metrics, and production scale strongly support the classification.

summary: Nik Caryotakis (SuperDial) shares lessons from scaling voice AI for healthcare phone call automation. SuperDial's core business is automating calls to insurance companies for mid-to-large healthcare administration businesses. Customers send call requests via CSV, API, or EHR integrations; SuperDial returns structured results within hours. Their agentic contract is results-based: customers pay for answers, not call attempts. If the bot cannot complete a call, a human fallback team handles it. SuperDial also learns from each call, updating office hours and phone tree traversal data. A prior authorization call demo illustrates a 'boring' but successful interaction. Key thesis: what differentiates voice agents isn't realistic voices or interruption handling—it's conversational content, design, and vertical integrations. New speech-to-speech models aren't production-ready because they output non-speech artifacts. SuperDial adopted PipeCat (open source, by Daily) for orchestration, choosing to self-host because calls can last up to 1.5 hours. They own their own OpenAI-compatible endpoint, routing generative responses through Tensor Zero for structured, typed LLM endpoints with fallback support. LaneFuse is self-hosted for logging, observability, anomaly detection, evals, and datasets—all HIPAA-compliant. TTS presents last-mile challenges: member IDs are 12-digit strings requiring precise pronunciation, and LLM output may not match desired audio. Tools like Rhyme help specify exact pronunciations; a spell function handles long words with appropriate pauses. Recordings are reviewed alongside transcripts. Persona naming matters: their bot was named 'Billy' (from 'SuperBill'), which caused phone confusion. Recommendations: don't build from scratch, track latency everywhere (time to first bite is critical), use Deepgram for STT with fine-tuning upgrade paths, have fallbacks ready for each stack component, and do end-to-end testing via fake phone numbers playing MP3s, simulated phone trees, and bot-to-bot testing with services like Koval. Conversation design shifted from prescriptive to descriptive; Kathy Pearl advised hiring conversation designers and doing table reads. Ethics matter: voice AI can be biased against accents and dialects.

sections.title: Intro & 2025 Voice AI Landscape
sections.summary: Nik introduces SuperDial and frames 2025 voice AI: fast affordable LLMs enabling complex conversations, realistic TTS with audio hallucination issues, and new voice-to-voice models that aren't production-ready due to non-speech output artifacts. SuperDial favors reliability over realism.

sections.title: SuperDial Product, Agentic Contract & Demo
sections.summary: SuperDial automates healthcare insurance calls for mid-to-large businesses. Customers send calls via CSV/API/EHR and receive structured results. The agentic contract is results-based with human fallback. A prior authorization demo shows a successful 'boring' call. System has saved 100,000+ hours with 4 engineers.

sections.title: Voice AI Engineer Role & Ethics
sections.summary: The voice AI engineer handles multimodal data, real-time latency, async/Python, and high conversational expectations. Two guiding sayings: 'say the right thing at the right time' and 'build this plane while we fly it.' Differentiation comes from conversation design and vertical integrations, not voice quality. Ethics: bias against accents/dialects, need for accessible collaborative tooling.

sections.title: Last Mile Problems, Conversation Design & PipeCat
sections.summary: Started with scrap STT/LLM/TTS pipeline. Conversation design shifted from prescriptive to descriptive. Kathy Pearl advised hiring conversation designers and doing table reads. SuperDial adopted PipeCat (open source by Daily) for orchestration—easy to extend for transfers and long phone calls.

sections.title: Stack Choices, TTS Last Mile & Testing Takeaways
sections.summary: PipeCat chosen for self-hosting (calls up to 1.5 hours). SuperDial owns an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, routes generative responses through Tensor Zero for typed LLM endpoints, and self-hosts LaneFuse for HIPAA-compliant logging/observability. TTS last-mile challenges: 12-digit member IDs, name pronunciation (Rhyme tool, spell function), recording review. Persona naming pitfall: 'Billy' confused over phone. Recommendations: don't build from scratch, track latency (time to first bite), use Deepgram with fine-tuning upgrade paths, have fallbacks for outages, and test end-to-end via MP3 playback, simulated phone trees, and bot-to-bot services like Koval. Final takeaways: choose stack wisely, focus on last mile, ride the wave of new models.

demonstrations: Prior authorization call demo: bot traverses phone tree, talks to human representative, asks about CPT code 81243, gets pending case status, reference number, and fax number for clinicals
limitations: Voice-to-voice/speech-to-speech models not production-ready—output non-speech artifacts
